title: Deserts of the World
summary: A world tour of deserts, from the hot Sahara to the cold Gobi, and how plants, animals, and people survive in them.
poll: Deserts are empty places with nothing worth studying.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:
A desert is dry. It gets no rain.

Not all deserts are hot. Some are cold. The Sahara is hot. The Gobi is cold. Both get no rain.

The Sahara has sand. Wind blows the sand. It makes hills. A hill of sand is a dune. Some dunes are tall.

Some deserts have rock, not sand. The ground there is hard.

A camel can live in a desert. It needs little water. Few plants grow there. But some still do.

A green spot with water is an oasis. Trees grow there. People rest there.

Long ago, traders used camels. They carried goods to sell. Today, people still live near deserts.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:
A desert gets almost no rain all year. That lack of rain is what makes it a desert.

Not every desert is hot. The Sahara is a hot desert in northern Africa. The Gobi is a cold desert in Asia with cold winters. Both deserts get very little rain.

Much of the Sahara is covered in soft sand. Strong winds blow the sand into tall hills. A hill of sand is called a dune. The Arabian Desert has huge dunes too.

Other deserts, like parts of the Gobi, are mostly rock, not sand. The ground is hard and often cracked.

A camel can live well in this dry land. It can go a long time with no water. Few plants can survive, but small bushes still grow.

A green spot with water is called an oasis. Trees grow around it, and people stop there to rest and drink.

Long ago, traders crossed deserts with camels to sell goods. Today, many people still live near deserts around the world.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:
A desert gets almost no rain, year after year. That lack of rain, not heat, is what truly makes it a desert.

Not every desert is hot. The Sahara is an enormous hot desert in northern Africa. The Gobi, on the other hand, is a cold desert in Asia with bitterly cold winters. Both deserts still get very little rain each year.

Much of the Sahara is covered in soft, fine sand. Strong winds blow the loose sand into tall, curving hills. A hill of sand is called a dune. The Arabian Desert, across the Middle East, also has huge rolling dunes.

Other deserts, like large parts of the Gobi, are mostly rock, not sand. The ground is hard, dry, and often cracked by heat and cold.

A camel can live surprisingly well in this dry land. It can go a long time with no drink of water. Few plants can survive, but small thorny bushes still grow.

A green spot with water in a desert is called an oasis. Trees grow around it, and people and animals stop there to rest and drink.

Long ago, traders crossed deserts with long lines of camels, carrying goods to sell between far cities. Today, many people still live near deserts all around the world.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:
Deserts look very different from each other. Some are covered in golden sand. Others are flat and covered in gray rock.

Yet every desert shares one thing. It gets very little rain. That is the real meaning of a dry, or arid, climate.

Deserts are found on every continent except Europe. The Sahara, in Africa, is the largest hot desert on Earth. The Arabian Desert covers much of the Middle East. The Gobi, in Asia, is a cold desert. Its winters can bring snow. So a desert does not have to be hot.

In sandy deserts like the Sahara, wind piles loose sand into huge dunes. The dunes slowly shift and change shape. In rocky deserts, wind and rare water wear down stone instead. This slow process is called erosion. It carves the rock into strange shapes.

Even in such harsh places, vegetation still grows. Thorny bushes and tough grasses can survive with little water. A camel can go for days without drinking. It stores fat that its body slowly turns into water.

An oasis is a spot where underground water reaches the surface. Trees and crops can grow there. For centuries, oases let traders rest safely as they crossed the sand.

Today, deserts are far from empty. Mines, farms, and growing cities depend on the resources found within them.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:

Yet every desert shares one true feature. It gets very little rainfall all year. That lack of rain, not heat, is the real meaning of a dry, or arid, climate.

Deserts are found on every continent except Europe. The Sahara, spread across northern Africa, is the largest hot desert on Earth. The Arabian Desert covers much of the Middle East, including large parts of Saudi Arabia. The Gobi, in Asia, is a cold desert, where winters bring freezing cold and even snow. So a desert does not have to be hot at all.

In sandy deserts like the Sahara, strong winds pile loose sand into huge dunes. The dunes slowly shift and change shape over time. In rocky deserts like parts of the Gobi, wind and rare water wear down stone instead. This slow process is called erosion. It carves the hard rock into strange, jagged shapes.

Even in such harsh places, vegetation still grows. Thorny bushes and tough grasses have learned to survive with very little water. A camel can go for many days without drinking. It stores fat that its body slowly turns into water when needed.

An oasis is a spot where underground water naturally reaches the surface. Trees and crops can grow there, and small towns can form nearby. For centuries, oases let traders and travelers rest safely as they crossed wide stretches of sand and rock.

Today, deserts are far from empty, lifeless places. Mines, farms near oases, and growing cities all depend on the resources found within these dry lands.

versions.title: Deserts of the World
versions.text:
Deserts look very different from one another across the whole world. Some are covered in golden sand that stretches for many miles. Others are flat and covered in gray rock and loose gravel instead.

Yet every desert shares one true feature. It receives very little rainfall all year long, and that lack of rain, far more than heat, is the real meaning of a dry, or arid, climate.

Deserts are found on every continent except Europe. The Sahara, spread across northern Africa, is the largest hot desert on Earth, almost as large as the entire United States. The Arabian Desert covers much of the Middle East, including large parts of Saudi Arabia, and has shaped the region's trade for thousands of years. The Gobi, in Asia, is a cold desert where winters bring freezing cold and even snow across its gravel plains. Far away in South America, the Atacama is thought to be the driest desert of all, since parts of it can go for years with no measurable rain. So a desert does not need to be hot; it only needs to be dry.

In sandy deserts like the Sahara, strong winds pile loose sand into huge dunes that slowly shift and change shape over months and years. In rocky deserts like parts of the Gobi and the Atacama, wind and rare water wear down stone instead through a slow process called erosion. It carves the hard rock into strange, jagged shapes.

Even in such harsh places, vegetation still grows. Thorny bushes and tough grasses have slowly adapted to survive with very little water. A camel can go for many days without drinking, because it stores fat that its body slowly turns into water when needed.

An oasis is a spot where underground water naturally reaches the surface, letting trees and crops grow there while small towns form nearby. For centuries, merchants on routes like the Silk Road relied on these oases to rest safely while carrying goods between faraway cities.

Today, deserts are far from empty, lifeless places. Mines, farms near oases, and fast-growing cities all depend on the resources found within these dry, remarkable lands.

versions.title: Deserts of the World: A Global Survey
versions.text:
Deserts look remarkably different from one another. One might be covered in golden sand, while another is flat gray rock. Yet geographers define a desert by one shared feature: an arid climate, meaning a region that receives extremely little precipitation each year, usually less than 250 millimeters.

Deserts exist on every continent except Europe. The Sahara, in northern Africa, is the largest hot desert on Earth. The Arabian Desert covers much of the Middle East, including large parts of Saudi Arabia, and has shaped trade there for thousands of years. The Gobi, in Asia, is a cold desert; its high elevation and distance from the sea keep its winters freezing. The Atacama, in South America, is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth, since a cold ocean current along its coast blocks the moist air that might bring rain.

In sandy deserts like the Sahara, winds pile loose sand into huge dunes that slowly shift over time. In rocky deserts like parts of the Gobi and Atacama, wind and rare water wear down stone through erosion instead, carving the ground into jagged shapes.

Despite the harsh conditions, deserts support real biodiversity. Thorny bushes, tough grasses, and small animals such as foxes and lizards have evolved traits that let them survive on very little water. Camels can go many days without drinking, storing fat that their bodies slowly convert into water.

Many desert peoples have traditionally lived a nomadic life, moving with their herds in search of grazing land, rather than settling in one place. An oasis forms where an aquifer, a layer of water-holding rock underground, brings water close enough to the surface for crops to grow. For centuries, merchants on routes like the Silk Road relied on these oases to rest safely.

Today, deserts are far from empty. Mines, farms near oases, and growing cities all depend on the resources found within these dry lands.

Deserts look remarkably different from one another across the entire globe, since one region might be covered in golden sand while another is flat gray rock and loose gravel instead. versions.title: Deserts of the World: A Global Survey
versions.text:
Deserts occupy nearly a third of Earth's entire land surface, yet they differ enormously from one another in appearance, climate, and the life they support across every inhabited continent except Europe. Geographers unite them under a single defining characteristic rather than temperature: an arid climate, one that receives extremely little precipitation annually, typically under 250 millimeters, regardless of whether the surrounding air feels scorching or bitterly cold throughout the changing seasons.

The Sahara, spanning northern Africa, stands as the largest hot desert on the planet, nearly as large as the entire United States, its sand dunes shaped continuously by prevailing winds into shifting, ever-changing formations across the generations. The Arabian Desert, covering much of the Middle East including substantial portions of Saudi Arabia, has influenced regional history and overland trade for untold millennia. The Gobi, by contrast, exemplifies a cold desert: its considerable elevation and remoteness from any ocean produce freezing winters despite minimal annual rainfall throughout the entire calendar year. Meanwhile, the Atacama Desert along South America's Pacific coast remains the driest nonpolar place on Earth, a persistent cold ocean current suppressing the evaporation that would otherwise generate rain-bearing clouds capable of drifting inland.

Erosion sculpts rocky deserts like portions of the Gobi and Atacama into jagged, wind-carved formations over immense stretches of geological time, while sandy deserts like the Sahara instead pile loose grains into dunes that migrate gradually across the landscape over decades and centuries. Despite such severe conditions, remarkable biodiversity persists throughout these environments: thorny vegetation, resilient grasses, and specially adapted animals such as foxes and lizards have evolved physical traits enabling survival with minimal available water. Camels exemplify this adaptation especially well, storing fat that their bodies metabolize into water precisely when hydration becomes necessary for continued survival.

Historically, many desert-dwelling peoples adopted nomadic lifestyles, migrating seasonally with livestock herds in pursuit of grazing land and dependable water rather than establishing permanent settlements in any single location. Oases emerge wherever underground aquifers, water-bearing rock layers lying beneath the dry surface, bring groundwater sufficiently close to sustain trees, crops, and small enduring communities nearby. For centuries, merchants traversing historic routes such as the Silk Road depended on these scattered havens to rest safely while transporting valuable goods between distant, prosperous cities spanning multiple continents and cultures.

Far from being empty or lifeless, deserts today sustain mines, oasis-adjacent farms, and rapidly expanding cities, all of which depend heavily on the mineral and groundwater resources concealed within these extraordinary, often misunderstood landscapes that continue to shape human settlement across the modern world.

versions.title: Deserts of the World: A Global Survey
versions.text:
Deserts occupy nearly a third of Earth's total land surface, yet they differ enormously from one another in appearance, climate, and the life forms they sustain, appearing on every inhabited continent except Europe. Geographers unite these varied landscapes under a single defining characteristic rather than temperature alone: an arid climate, one that receives extremely little precipitation annually, typically under 250 millimeters, regardless of whether the surrounding air feels scorching hot or bitterly cold throughout the changing seasons of the year.

The Sahara, spanning the entirety of northern Africa, stands as the largest hot desert on the planet, nearly as large as the entire United States, its countless sand dunes continuously reshaped by prevailing winds into shifting, ever-changing formations across generations of travelers. The Arabian Desert, covering much of the Middle East including substantial portions of Saudi Arabia, has profoundly influenced regional history and overland trade for untold millennia. The Gobi, by striking contrast, exemplifies a cold desert: its considerable elevation and remoteness from any ocean produce consistently freezing winters despite minimal annual rainfall throughout the entire calendar year. Meanwhile, the Atacama Desert along South America's Pacific coast remains the driest nonpolar place on Earth, a persistent cold ocean current suppressing the evaporation that would otherwise generate rain-bearing clouds capable of reaching the arid interior.

Erosion gradually sculpts rocky deserts like portions of the Gobi and Atacama into jagged, wind-carved formations over immense stretches of geological time, while sandy deserts like the Sahara instead accumulate loose grains into dunes that migrate slowly across the landscape over decades and even centuries. Despite such severe and unforgiving conditions, remarkable biodiversity persists throughout these environments: thorny vegetation, resilient grasses, and specially adapted animals such as foxes and lizards have evolved distinctive physical traits enabling survival with strikingly minimal available water. Camels exemplify this adaptation especially well, storing fat that their bodies metabolize gradually into water precisely when hydration becomes physiologically necessary for their continued survival.

Historically, many desert-dwelling peoples adopted nomadic lifestyles, migrating seasonally alongside livestock herds in pursuit of grazing land and dependable water rather than establishing permanent settlements in any single fixed location. Oases emerge wherever underground aquifers, water-bearing rock layers lying beneath the parched surface, bring groundwater sufficiently close to sustain trees, crops, and small enduring communities nearby. For centuries, merchants traversing historic routes such as the Silk Road depended entirely on these scattered havens to rest safely while transporting valuable goods between distant, prosperous cities spanning multiple continents and cultures.

Far from being empty or lifeless wastelands, deserts today sustain mines, oasis-adjacent farms, and rapidly expanding cities, all of which depend heavily on the mineral and groundwater resources concealed within these extraordinary, often profoundly misunderstood landscapes that continue to shape patterns of human settlement across the modern world.

MID.modelAnswer: A place does not have to be hot to be a desert. The article says a desert is defined by how little rain it gets, not its temperature. The Sahara is a hot desert in Africa, while the Gobi in Asia is a cold desert with freezing winters. Both deserts, however, get very little rain each year, which is the real reason both are called deserts.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says deserts are empty places with nothing worth studying. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article about desert climate, biodiversity, and human history.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that deserts are empty places with nothing worth studying. Deserts around the world, from the hot Sahara to the cold Gobi and the extremely dry Atacama, show that aridity rather than temperature truly defines a desert, which is itself a fascinating scientific idea. Deserts also support real biodiversity, including hardy vegetation and animals like foxes, lizards, and camels that have evolved clever adaptations to survive with very little water. Someone might argue that deserts are lifeless because few people live there, but oases fed by underground aquifers have supported nomadic peoples and merchant trade routes like the Silk Road for centuries, proving that deserts have shaped human history in important ways.
